summary.text: Earth's mantle is the layer of silicate rock between the crust and the outer core, holding 67% of Earth's mass and 84% of its volume.
It is mostly solid, yet over geologic time it flows like a thick fluid, and this slow convection is thought to be an integral part of how plates move.
Partial melting of the mantle makes new crust: oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges and continental crust at subduction zones.

facts.label: Temperature range
facts.value: About 500 K at the top to 4,200 K at the bottom

facts.label: Top boundary
facts.value: The Moho, first noted by Mohorovičić in 1909

items.prompt: Deep mantle rock is far hotter than the temperature at which the same rock melts at the surface. Why does it stay almost entirely solid?

options.label: Huge pressure raises the temperature it needs to melt
The rock there contains no iron to melt
Water in the rock keeps it cool
Heat flows out too fast to build up

items.explain: The enormous pressure on the mantle prevents melting, because the temperature at which melting begins rises with pressure.

items.prompt: Mantle rock is solid, yet over millions of years it slowly flows. Which everyday material has been used to describe its consistency?
items.explain: The mantle is predominantly solid but behaves as a viscous fluid on geologic time scales, sometimes likened to caramel.

items.prompt: Rock near the bottom of the mantle is heated far more than the rock above it. What happens over millions of years?

options.label: It stays put and melts into a lake
It sinks deeper into the core
Hot rock slowly rises while cooler rock sinks
It cracks apart and turns to gas

items.explain: The temperature difference and slow creep of hot rock drive convection: hot material rises in plumes while cooler, heavier material sinks.

items.prompt: Seismic images show two continent-sized dense zones at the bottom of the mantle. What is one proposed origin for them?

options.label: Remains of the body whose impact made the Moon

items.explain: These anomalies may be buried relics of mantle from Theia, left after the Moon-forming impact in the giant-impact hypothesis.

items.prompt: A geologist wants to hold real mantle rock without drilling deep into the Earth. Where is a good place to look?
items.explain: Mantle rock can be sampled as xenoliths, pieces embedded in basalts or kimberlites as they form, or in ophiolites pushed onto continents.

items.prompt: A plume of hot mantle rock rises under a spot far from any plate edge. What would you expect to find on the surface above it?

options.label: A sinking basin with no volcanoes

items.explain: Hot, less dense plume rock is buoyant, so places above plumes are predicted to sit high and show hot spot volcanism.
